q: MAE vs RMSE: which and when?
a: MAE: average absolute miss in target units, robust to outliers, optimal prediction is the median. RMSE: squares errors, so large misses dominate; optimal prediction is the mean. Use RMSE when big errors are disproportionately costly; MAE when you want typical error and have outliers. RMSE ≥ MAE always; a big gap means some large errors.

q: What are the problems with MAPE?
a: Undefined or explodes when actuals are zero or tiny; asymmetric (over-forecasts can give unbounded %, under-forecasts are capped at 100%), so optimising it biases forecasts low; small items dominate. Use WAPE, sMAPE, or MASE.

Skewed targets spanning orders of magnitude (prices, counts), when relative error matters more than absolute, and when under-prediction should be penalised a bit more than over-prediction. It's RMSE on log1p of the values.

q: Which loss gives median predictions and which gives mean predictions?
a: Absolute error (L1) → median. Squared error (L2) → mean. Quantile (pinball) loss with τ → the τ-th quantile, e.g. τ = 0.9 for a P90 forecast.

q: What does R² actually tell you?
a: The share of variance in y explained by the model compared with predicting the mean. It doesn't say whether predictions are unbiased or errors acceptable in business units, and it can be high with a useless model on trending data. Report it with MAE/RMSE.
